content: Hepatitis refers to a condition characterized by damage to the liver, which is marked by the presence of inflammatory cells within the liver tissue. This condition can either resolve on its own without intervention or progress to liver scarring, also known as fibrosis. Hepatitis is classified as acute if it lasts less than six months, and chronic if it persists beyond this duration. The majority of liver damage cases worldwide are caused by a group of viruses collectively referred to as hepatitis viruses. However, hepatitis can also result from exposure to toxins, such as alcohol, other infections, or autoimmune processes. In some cases, the disease may follow a subclinical course, meaning the affected individual may not exhibit any noticeable symptoms or feel unwell. When the disease progresses to impair liver function, the patient may develop symptoms. The liver's essential functions include filtering harmful substances, regulating blood composition, and producing bile to aid in digestion. The term hepatitis is derived from the ancient Greek word hepar (ἧπαρ) or hepato(ἡπατο-), meaning liver, combined with the suffix -itis, which denotes inflammation. World Hepatitis Awareness Day is an annual event organized by various global advocacy groups to raise awareness about infectious hepatitis, promote efforts to curb its spread, and advocate for the treatment of those affected. In the United States, hepatitis A virus (HAV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), hepatitis D virus (HDV, which coexists with HBV infection), and hepatitis E virus (HEV) collectively account for 95% of all cases of acute viral hepatitis. Computed tomography (CT) imaging of the abdomen may be performed to rule out other potential causes of hepatitis, such as biliary obstruction. It is also used to evaluate the progression of hepatitis to more severe conditions, such as cirrhosis or liver carcinoma.
